## The question

Hurricane Katrina reached Louisiana on August 29, 2005. It killed 1,392
people and caused 125 billion dollars of damage. Sixteen years later to
the day, Hurricane Ida reached the same coast with winds of 240 km/h.

The National Hurricane Center forecasts every Atlantic storm every six
hours. A forecast says where the centre of the storm will be and how
strong its wind will be, up to five days ahead. Around the forecast track
the Center draws a cone. The cone is as wide as the Center's own errors
of the five years before, so the storm stays inside it about two times
out of three.

People act on these forecasts. They leave, protect their homes and move
goods, and a wrong forecast costs money and lives. Martinez
([Econometrics, 2020](https://doi.org/10.3390/econometrics8020018)) finds
that hurricanes whose landfall was forecast with a larger error caused
more damage. Molina & Rudik
([NBER Working Paper 32548, 2024](https://doi.org/10.3386/w32548)) find
that better forecasts since 2007 cut the cost of a hurricane by 23%,
about 2 billion dollars a storm.

Have the forecasts become more accurate? In this homework you measure the
error of every official forecast from 1970 to 2025. Then you compare two
forecasts made on August 26, three days before the storm reached
Louisiana: Katrina's in 2005 and Ida's in 2021.

This is a spatial problem: distances between points, a polygon built from
circles, a point inside a polygon, and a grid summed inside a polygon.

## Data

All of it is public and needs no key.

1. **Forecasts, from the National Hurricane Center (one file per
   storm).** A file holds every forecast made for a storm, by the Center
   and by each computer model. Read
   [the notes on the archive](https://ftp.nhc.noaa.gov/atcf/README) and
   [what each field of a line is](https://science.nrlmry.navy.mil/atcf/docs/database/new/abdeck.txt).
   There is one folder per year, from 1970 to 2025. The Atlantic files
   start with `aal`. The second address is Katrina, storm 12 of 2005,
   which the best track calls `AL122005`.

   ```text
   https://ftp.nhc.noaa.gov/atcf/archive/2005/
   https://ftp.nhc.noaa.gov/atcf/archive/2005/aal122005.dat.gz
   ```

   Keep the lines of the technique `OFCL`, the Center's own forecast. A
   file repeats a forecast on several lines: keep one line for each
   storm, start of the forecast and hours ahead. A latitude of 0 means no
   position was forecast, and a wind of 0 means no wind was forecast.

2. **Best track, from the National Hurricane Center (one text file).**
   The Center's final record of each storm: its position, its status and
   its maximum sustained wind every six hours. Read
   [how the file is laid out](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/hurdat/hurdat2-format-atl-1851-2021.pdf).

   ```text
   https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/hurdat/hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt
   ```

3. **A cone the Center published (a shapefile in a zip).** The cone of
   Hurricane Milton, advisory 12, made public on October 7, 2024 at
   10 pm CDT. The cone is the file `al142024-012_5day_pgn.shp`. Read
   [how the Center defines the cone](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/aboutcone.shtml).

   ```text
   https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/gis/forecast/archive/al142024_5day_012.zip
   ```

4. **Population, from the Global Human Settlement Layer (tiles).** The
   number of people in each cell of 30 arc-seconds, about 1 km, every
   five years
   ([description](https://human-settlement.emergency.copernicus.eu/ghs_pop2023.php)).
   A tile covers 10 by 10 degrees. You need rows 6 and 7 and columns 9 to
   11 of 2005, and rows 6 to 8 and the same columns of 2020. This is row
   7, column 10 of 2020; for 2005, write `E2005` in place of `E2020` in
   both places. The server is slow: raise R's time limit for a download
   with `options(timeout = 900)`.

   ```text
   https://jeodpp.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ftp/jrc-opendata/GHSL/GHS_POP_GLOBE_R2023A/GHS_POP_E2020_GLOBE_R2023A_4326_30ss/V1-0/tiles/GHS_POP_E2020_GLOBE_R2023A_4326_30ss_V1_0_R7_C10.zip
   ```

5. **Map layers.**

   The states, from the Census Bureau
   ([description](https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/cartographic-boundary.html)):

   ```text
   https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2023/shp/cb_2023_us_state_20m.zip
   ```

   The land, from Natural Earth
   ([description](https://www.naturalearthdata.com/downloads/50m-physical-vectors/50m-land/)):

   ```text
   https://naciscdn.org/naturalearth/50m/physical/ne_50m_land.zip
   ```

## The errors

- Compare each forecast position with the best track at the time the
  forecast was for: its start plus its hours. A forecast belongs to the
  year it starts in.
- The **distance error** is the distance between the forecast position
  and the actual one, in km, along the Earth's surface (`st_distance()`
  on longitude and latitude).
- The **wind speed error** is the difference between the forecast wind
  and the actual one, without its sign, in km/h. A knot is 1.852 km/h.
  The archive has wind forecasts from 1990.
- Count a forecast when the best track calls the storm `TS`, `SS` or `HU`
  both at the start of the forecast and at the time it was for.
- Panels C and D show a five-year average at 24, 48 and 72 hours: for
  each year, the average over all the forecasts of that year, the two
  years before and the two years after. At both ends of the series, use
  the years there are.
- For the forecasts of 2005 alone, my average distance error at 72 hours
  is 278.0 km, over 242 forecasts. For 2021 alone it is 113.8 km, over
  138 forecasts.

## The cones

Build each cone yourself. The Center's archive of cones starts in 2008,
after Katrina.

- **Radius.** For a storm of year *y*, take the forecasts of the five
  years before *y*. The radius at a lead time is the distance error that
  two-thirds of them stayed under (the 2/3 quantile). For the radii, also
  count the forecasts where the storm was a depression, `TD` or `SD`, at
  either time. The radius at the start of a forecast is 30 km (16
  nautical miles).
- **Shape.** Take the forecast positions at 0, 12, 24, 36, 48 and 72
  hours. Fill in every hour between them: the position along a smooth
  curve through the six positions, the radius along a straight line
  between lead times. Draw a circle each hour. The cone is the area the
  circles sweep. Work on a flat map in metres centred on the forecast. I
  used a natural spline and an azimuthal equidistant projection.
- **Check.** Build the cone of Milton's forecast that starts on October
  8, 2024 at 00:00 UTC (storm 14 of 2024), with the positions at 96 and
  120 hours added, and compare it with the Center's shapefile. The
  overlap is the area both cones cover, divided by the area either
  covers. It must be above 95%. Mine is 98.6%.
- My radii at 24, 48 and 72 hours are 144, 267 and 386 km for 2005, and
  73, 127 and 189 km for 2021.

## The two forecasts

- **Katrina**, storm 12 of 2005: the forecast that starts on August 26 at
  12:00 UTC.
- **Ida**, storm 9 of 2021: the forecast that starts on August 26 at
  18:00 UTC.
- For each, after 24, 48 and 72 hours: the distance error, the wind speed
  error, and whether the storm was inside the cone.
- For each, the **US residents inside the cone**: the sum of the
  population grid over the part of the cone inside the lower 48 states
  of the Census file (all states but Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico).
  Use the grid of 2005 for Katrina and of 2020 for Ida.

The first run, on a MacBook Pro with an M2 Max chip:

| Step | Minutes | Downloaded |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Download the 762 forecast files | about 6 | 339 MB |
| Read them and keep the official forecasts | 2 | |
| Download the best track and measure the errors | under 1 | 7 MB |
| Build the cones and check Milton's | under 1 | |
| Download the population tiles and count the residents | 1 | 69 MB |
| Draw the figure | under 1 | |
| **Total** | **about 10** | **415 MB** |

Save each file you download. A second run then takes about two minutes.

- `figures/hw7_target.png`, about 14 × 14.4 inches at 200 dpi.
- `data_clean/storms.csv`: one row per storm and day, six rows, with
  `distance_km`, `wind_error_kmh`, `radius_km` and `inside_cone`.
- `data_clean/yearly_errors.csv`: one row per year and lead time, with

## What the figure says

After three days, Ida's forecast was 33 km off and Katrina's 319 km.
Over the three days, Ida's wind speed errors were as large as Katrina's.
In `NOTES.md`, say in two or three sentences what panels C and D show
about each error since 1990.

## Figure rules

- The figure has one title, a dark background and one line of sources at
  the bottom. Titles, labels and colours are those of the target.
- **Panels A and B**, the same area at the same scale: longitude -96.5
  to -76, latitude 15.8 to 34.4. Behind each map, the people per km² in
  2020 in four classes (from 1, 10, 100 and 1,000) and the sea in blue.
  For the density, add up the people of 3 by 3 cells and divide by their
  area. On each map: the cone and the forecast track to 72 hours, the
  actual track from the start of the forecast to 78 hours later, and a
  bar from the forecast position to the actual one after 1, 2 and 3
  days. The days, the start of the forecast, the landfall in Louisiana
  and New Orleans are labelled. Map A has two keys and both maps have a
  scale.
- **Under each map**, a table: the distance error and the wind speed
  error after 1, 2 and 3 days, and the US residents inside the cone.
- **Panels C and D**, one line per lead time, labelled at its end, with
  the two forecasts marked. Panel D has the years of panel C: its lines
  start in 1990 and the years before are shaded.
- C sits under A and D under B, with the same left and right edges.

## Commits

Commit each step when it works. A healthy history for a project like
this has a series of commits. For example:

1. The project organized: folders, `.gitignore`, `code/run_everything.R`.
2. The code that gets the data: forecasts and best track.
3. The code that measures the errors.
4. The cones and the check against the Center's.
5. The residents inside each cone.
6. Panels A and B, with their tables.
7. Panels C and D.
8. A last pass that cleans up the code.

This order is just an example. You can adopt your own workflow.

## How to submit

Your repository is **`hw7-<your github username>`** in the course
organization. Put the code in `code/`, with `code/run_everything.R`
running it all, and paths relative to the project root. Push the code,
the two tables, the figure, `NOTES.md`, and the files your figure script
reads (the cones, the tracks and the map layers, under 25 MB in all). The
grader downloads nothing, so the script that draws the figure must run
from a fresh clone. The grader uses the last commit pushed before the
deadline.

Recommended. Ask for the script rather than the answer, check what it
